keyframe_review.note: 295 cells, 0 in Canada and the United States. Nothing here is New France after the Treaty of Paris; a region minus itself is used as the empty shape. Saint-Domingue and French Guiana have dossiers (saint-domingue, french-colony-of-guiana); the other overseas pieces need one (see notes).

correction.text: No New France in 1791; the 438 km2 shape (Saint Pierre and Miquelon and a few cells on the Mississippi) is the same one Cliopatria gives to its 'First French colonial empire' row for 1805-1814, and France recovered the two islands in 1763 (the Treaty of Paris page: France recovered the two small islands from Britain)

keyframe_review.note: 438.6 km2, 16 vertices, 0 resolvable cells: Saint Pierre and Miquelon plus a sliver in the United States. France kept the islands at the Treaty of Paris but New France had ended; the islands need a French-colonies dossier (saint-pierre-and-miquelon).

region.text: Saint Croix Island (1604) and Port-Royal (1605), Acadia

ledger.note: 1604: the French settle Saint Croix Island, the first colony of New France. Acadia page: 'under the authority of the French King, Henri IV, on Saint Croix Island in 1604'; 'The first capital of Acadia was established in 1605 as Port-Royal'; 'the last of the French left Port Royal in August 1607' and in 1610 the habitation stood 'just as it was left', so 1607-1610 is a claim without a garrison. New France page: 'In 1604, King Henri IV sponsored Pierre Dugua, Sieur de Mons to found a settlement in New France.'

region.text: Quebec on the Saint Lawrence

ledger.note: 1608: Champlain founds Quebec. New France page: 'In 1608, King Henry IV sponsored Pierre Dugua, Sieur de Mons and Samuel de Champlain as founders of' Quebec (the quotation breaks off before the name; the page's own heading and the infobox 'Capital: Quebec' give it).
1608: the seat of New France moves from Acadia to Quebec, the capital the infobox gives ('Capital: Quebec', no years on the page).

1627: New France passes to the Company of One Hundred Associates. 'In 1627, Richelieu founded the Company of One Hundred Associates to invest in New France.' An administrative change; no land moves and the colour continues. The page gives no dissolution date for the company; 1663 ends its control.

region.text: Acadia and Cape Breton Island

ledger.note: 1629: the English also hold Acadia and Cape Breton Island. The treaty page says the English 'had seized' New France in 1629 and the 1632 treaty 'returned New France (Quebec, Acadia and Cape Breton Island)'; the Acadia page dates English control from 1621 and the Cape Breton page has French settlements at Englishtown (1629) and St. Peter's (1630), so the exact year and holder of the two lands is the page's but my reading.

region.text: Quebec

ledger.note: 1629 (19 July): Quebec surrenders to the English. 'On 19 July 1629, an English fleet under the command of David Kirke managed to cause the surrender of Quebec', cutting off supplies until Champlain's men were starving; the page adds that this followed the treaty of Susa and 'was considered illegitimate'.

region.text: Quebec, Acadia and Cape Breton Island

ledger.note: 1632 (29 March): the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye gives New France back. 'The Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye was signed on March 29, 1632'; it 'returned New France (Quebec, Acadia and Cape Breton Island) to French control after the English had seized it in 1629'.

region.text: the Saint Lawrence valley from Trois-Rivieres to Montreal

ledger.note: 1642: the Saint Lawrence settlement runs up to Montreal. Cliopatria adds 28 cells between Quebec and Montreal; none of the pages opened dates the founding of Montreal, so this is a bridge over a silence (the New France page names only 'the districts of Quebec, Trois-Rivières, and Montreal').

region.text: Acadia, the Port-Royal region, without Cape Breton

ledger.note: 1654: the English take Acadia again. Acadia page: England held it 'again from 1654 until 1670' (the page is silent on the Treaty of Breda of 1667). The land is the Acadia cells of Cliopatria's 1653 shape, my reading; Cape Breton stays French to 1659.

region.text: Cape Breton Island

ledger.note: 1659: Cape Breton Island falls empty. The French settlements 'lasted only one generation, until Nicolas Denys left in 1659' and the island 'did not have any European settlers for another fifty years'.

region.text: Placentia Bay, Newfoundland (Plaisance)

ledger.note: 1662: Plaisance on Newfoundland's Placentia Bay. 'They built Fort Plaisance in 1662.' The page also says the French 'made Placentia (French: Plaisance) their capital' in 1655, which Cliopatria does not follow.

1663: New France becomes a royal province. 'In 1663, New France finally became more secure when' (page) ... 'Louis XIV made it a royal province, taking control away from the Company of One Hundred Associates'. An administrative change; no land moves.

region.text: the Sault Sainte Marie mission

ledger.note: 1668: the Sault Sainte Marie mission, the first French post on the upper Great Lakes. Page: 'the Mission of Sault Sainte Marie in 1668'. Cliopatria draws two cells from 1670.

region.text: Acadia, the Port-Royal region and the Bay of Fundy shore

ledger.note: 1670: Acadia returns to France. Acadia page: England held it 'again from 1654 until 1670'; the page is silent on the Treaty of Breda (1667). Cliopatria draws the larger Acadia (60 cells) from 1673.

region.text: the Michilimackinac mission, Straits of Mackinac

ledger.note: 1671: the Michilimackinac mission. 'In 1671, Father Jacques Marquette established a French mission at Michilimackinac.' Cliopatria draws the cells from 1683.

region.text: Fort Frontenac, the head of the Saint Lawrence at Lake Ontario

ledger.note: 1673: Fort Frontenac on Lake Ontario. The page lists 'Fort Frontenac (1673)'; Cliopatria's Saint Lawrence shape reaches the lake from 1673. Whose land it was the page does not say (the Haudenosaunee touch New France from 1642 in the neighbour list).

region.text: Green Bay, Lake Michigan

ledger.note: 1673: Cliopatria draws four cells at Green Bay. The Illinois Country page has Marquette and Jolliet exploring 'from Green Bay to the Arkansas River' in 1673, not a post; Fort La Baye is dated 1717 on the Pays d'en Haut page. A bridge over a silence.

region.text: the Saint Lawrence valley and Ottawa River

ledger.note: 1677: the Saint Lawrence shape grows from 93 to 120 cells; no page opened dates it.

region.text: Fort Niagara at the mouth of the Niagara River

ledger.note: 1678: Fort Niagara. The page lists 'Fort Niagara (1678)'; Cliopatria draws the Niagara cells from 1687.

region.text: Fort Saint Louis on the Illinois River

ledger.note: 1682: Fort Saint Louis on the Illinois River, the Illinois Country's first lasting post. La Salle built Fort St. Louis on the Illinois River 'in the winter of 1682'. The Louisiana page: 'Established: 1682' for the colony, and in April 1682 La Salle 'arrived at the mouth of the Mississippi' and claimed the basin; Cliopatria draws no Louisiana until 1686, so the claim is not a gain here.

region.text: the Saint Lawrence valley and Ottawa River

ledger.note: 1683: the Saint Lawrence shape grows again (120 to 136 cells); no page opened dates it.

region.text: Arkansas Post on the Arkansas River

ledger.note: 1686: Arkansas Post. '1686: Henri de Tonti establishes Arkansas Post, a trading post at the site of a Quapaw Indian village.'

region.text: the Hudson's Bay Company posts along James Bay

ledger.note: 1686 (March): New France strikes the English posts on James Bay. 'In March 1686 the French sent a raiding party under the Chevalier de Troyes' against 'the HBC posts along James Bay'.

region.text: the Hudson's Bay Company posts along James Bay

ledger.note: 1686 (March): the James Bay posts are taken. The page does not name the posts the raiders captured; it says 'The French retained all of the outposts except Fort Albany until 1713'. Cliopatria draws seven cells at 51.7 N 81.5 W from 1687.

region.text: a Texas coast post and a Wisconsin post

ledger.note: 1687: three cells on the Texas coast and a Wisconsin dot appear in Cliopatria's shape; none of the pages opened mentions them. The Texas cells leave in 1691.

region.text: the Texas coast post

ledger.note: 1691: the Texas cells leave Cliopatria's shape; page silent.

region.text: Cahokia on the east bank of the Mississippi

ledger.note: 1696: Cahokia. Cahokia was 'established in 1696 by French missionaries from Quebec'; Kaskaskia follows in 1703. Cliopatria draws the Cahokia cells from 1700.

region.text: York Factory on Hudson Bay

ledger.note: 1697 (5 September): d'Iberville's second raid on York Factory. 'In 1697, d'Iberville again commanded a French naval raid on York Factory' (the page names 'the Battle of Hudson's Bay (5 September 1697)'); he had taken it in 1694 but 'the company recovered it the next year'. Cliopatria draws the York Factory cells from 1696.

region.text: Fort Maurepas at Old Biloxi

ledger.note: 1699: Old Biloxi. '1699: Pierre Le Moyne, Sieur d'Iberville explores the Louisiana coast and founds Fort Maurepas at Old Biloxi.'

region.text: Fort Pontchartrain du Detroit

ledger.note: 1701: Detroit. 'In 1701, Antoine Laumet de La Mothe founded Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit.'

region.text: Mobile and its bay

ledger.note: 1702 (January): Mobile. '1702: In January, Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, Sieur de Bienville founds Mobile'; it is the Louisiana capital to 1720 (infobox 'Mobile (1702-1720)').

region.text: peninsular Nova Scotia, the Acadian capital Port Royal

ledger.note: 1710: the British take Port-Royal. 'Acadia was conquered in 1710 during Queen Anne's War'; the page does not name Nicholson. The conquest is 'confirmed by the Treaty of Utrecht of 1713'.

region.text: Cape Breton Island (Ile Royale)

ledger.note: 1713: Cape Breton, as Ile Royale, is French again and Louisbourg is founded. 'Louisbourg was founded in 1713'; the Utrecht page: France 'retained its other pre-war North American possessions, including Cape Breton Island'. The island had been empty since 1659.

region.text: peninsular Nova Scotia

ledger.note: 1713 (April): the occupation of peninsular Nova Scotia ends in cession. 'The 1710 conquest of the Acadian capital of Port Royal during the war was confirmed by the Treaty of Utrecht of 1713.'

region.text: peninsular Nova Scotia (mainland Acadia)

ledger.note: 1713 (11 April): Utrecht cedes Nova Scotia. 'The main treaties of peace followed on 11 April 1713'; France 'ceded Nova Scotia and its claims to Newfoundland and territories in Rupert's Land'. Acadia page: mainland Nova Scotia 'Lost to Great Britain in 1713'; New Brunswick and Maine stay French to 1763.

region.text: Plaisance and the French claims on Newfoundland

ledger.note: 1713 (11 April): Utrecht cedes France's claims to Newfoundland. The Placentia page: 'the Treaty of Utrecht forced the French to abandon their Placentia Bay settlements'; the residents were shipped to Louisbourg in 1714.

region.text: the Hudson Bay and James Bay posts

ledger.note: 1713 (April): the Hudson Bay contest ends. After the Treaty of Utrecht the page has France 'relinquish all claims to Great Britain on the Hudson Bay'.

region.text: the Hudson Bay and James Bay posts

ledger.note: 1713 (April): the Hudson Bay posts go to Britain. 'The French retained all of the outposts except Fort Albany until 1713'; Utrecht 'required France to relinquish all claims to Great Britain on the Hudson Bay'.

region.text: Natchitoches on the Red River

ledger.note: 1714: Natchitoches. '1714: Louis Juchereau de St. Denis founds Natchitoches.'

region.text: Fort Rosalie at Natchez

ledger.note: 1716: Fort Rosalie at Natchez. '1716: Fort Rosalie is established on a bluff overlooking the Mississippi River.'

region.text: New Orleans on the Mississippi

ledger.note: 1718: New Orleans. '1718: New Orleans is founded, at a crescent in the river, for protection against flooding.' The seat of government moves to Biloxi in 1720 and to New Orleans in 1722.

region.text: a post in Alabama and a cluster of posts around the head of Lake Michigan

ledger.note: 1718: Cliopatria adds a dot in Alabama (32.8 N 86.6 W) and a cluster at 41.1 N 86.3 W on the Michigan-Indiana line; none of the pages opened mentions them. The Louisiana page has '1717: Illinois Country is detached from Canada to be governed by Louisiana (Haute-Louisiane)', an administrative change that moves no border.

region.text: Ile Saint-Jean, Prince Edward Island

ledger.note: 1721: Ile Saint-Jean (Prince Edward Island) joins Cliopatria's shape. The Ile-Royale page says the colony 'consisted of two main islands' and describes the second as present-day Prince Edward Island, without a year.

region.text: the lower Mississippi and Gulf coast settlements

ledger.note: 1721: the Louisiana shape thickens from 75 to 170 cells along the Mississippi and the Gulf coast; the Louisiana page dates posts, not this growth (Crozat 1712 to 1731 and the Company years are undated on it).

region.text: Fort Beauharnois on Lake Pepin and the upper Mississippi

ledger.note: 1727: Fort Beauharnois on the upper Mississippi. The page lists 'Fort Beauharnois (1727)'.

region.text: Fort St. Pierre on Rainy Lake

ledger.note: 1731: Fort Saint-Pierre on Rainy Lake. La Vérendrye left Montreal in 1731 and 'that autumn his son Jean-Baptiste built Fort St. Pierre on Rainy Lake' (the year is the page's sentence order).

region.text: Fort St. Charles on Lake of the Woods

ledger.note: 1732: Fort Saint-Charles on Lake of the Woods, La Vérendrye's headquarters. 'Next year they built Fort St. Charles on Lake of the Woods, which became his headquarters.'

region.text: Fort Maurepas near the mouth of the Red River at the southern end of Lake Winnipeg

ledger.note: 1734: Fort Maurepas on Lake Winnipeg. 'In 1734 their party reached Lake Winnipeg' and Jean-Baptiste 'built Fort Maurepas near the mouth of the Red River'.

region.text: the Gaspe, New Brunswick and Maine claim between Canada and Acadia

ledger.note: 1734: Cliopatria's big cluster grows from 147 to 322 cells, filling the ground between Canada, New Brunswick and Maine. No page opened dates it; the Acadia page says New Brunswick and Maine east of the Kennebec were 'Lost to Great Britain in 1763', so the claim itself is French.

region.text: Fort La Reine, Portage la Prairie, south of Lake Manitoba

ledger.note: 1738 (October): Fort La Reine. La Vérendrye 'built Fort La Reine just south of Lake Manitoba (October 1738)'.

region.text: the lakes of Manitoba west of Lake Winnipeg

ledger.note: 1741: Cliopatria adds 13 cells in Manitoba (Lake Winnipeg to 101 W). The page names Fort Dauphin, Fort Bourbon and Fort Paskoya but dates none of them, and records the sons' ride to the Rockies in 1742-43.

region.text: Forts Presque Isle, Le Boeuf and Duquesne, the Ohio Country

ledger.note: 1753: Fort Presque Isle and Fort Le Boeuf, then Fort Duquesne in 1754, carry New France into the Ohio Country. The page lists 'Fort Presque Isle (1753)', 'Fort Le Boeuf (1753)' and 'Fort Duquesne (1754)'. Cliopatria draws the Pennsylvania cells from 1757.

region.text: the Ohio Country and the forks of the Ohio

ledger.note: 1754 (April): the Ohio Country is fought for. The French fort at the forks of the Ohio: 'These forces arrived at the fort on April 16, but Contrecoeur generously allowed Trent's small company to withdraw'; in May 1754 'the Battle of Jumonville Glen' follows.

region.text: the Isthmus of Chignecto around Fort Beauséjour

ledger.note: 1755 (June): Fort Beauséjour falls. 'Colonel Monckton captured Fort Beauséjour in June 1755'; the Acadian deportation 'beginning in 1755' follows. The land is the Isthmus of Chignecto, my reading; Cliopatria keeps the New Brunswick cells to 1761.

region.text: Ile Royale (Cape Breton Island) and Louisbourg

ledger.note: 1758 (26 July): Louisbourg falls to the British. 'On 26 July 1758, after the second Siege of Louisbourg' the governor gave the keys to the British; the page's infobox: 'Under British military occupation (1758-1763)'.

region.text: Quebec and its district, the city that surrendered

ledger.note: 1759 (September): Quebec falls. 'In September 1759, James Wolfe defeated Montcalm in the Battle of the Plains of Abraham' and 'the French capitulated the city to the British' (the page gives no day for either).

minus.text: Quebec and its district, the city that surrendered

region.text: Canada beyond Quebec: the Saint Lawrence valley, the Great Lakes posts, the Ohio forts and Acadia's remnant

ledger.note: 1760 (8 September): Montreal capitulates and Canada passes under British military occupation. 'De Lévis and the Marquis de Vaudreuil reluctantly signed the Articles of Capitulation of Montreal on September 8'; 'General Amherst also oversaw the transfer of French fortifications to British control on the western frontier'. The New France page: 'Colony under British military occupation (1760-1763)'.

region.text: the Ohio Country

ledger.note: 1760 (8 September): the Ohio fighting ends with the capitulation of Montreal; the page records Fort Duquesne's fall in neither month nor year (it dates only 'the Forbes Expedition ... in September-October 1758').

region.text: Louisiana west of the Mississippi with New Orleans

ledger.note: 1762 (November): France cedes Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain. 'In the 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau, France ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi River to Spain.' The Treaty of Paris page says France 'had already secretly given Louisiana to Spain three months earlier' than 10 February 1763, which gives November; the page keeps New Orleans and its island French in the Paris text (Article VII) although they had already gone to Spain, so New Orleans is included in the ceded land here.

region.text: Ile Royale (Cape Breton Island) and Louisbourg

ledger.note: 1763 (10 February): the British occupation of Ile Royale ends in cession.

region.text: Quebec and its district, the city that surrendered

ledger.note: 1763 (10 February): the occupation of Quebec ends in cession.

minus.text: Quebec and its district, the city that surrendered

region.text: Canada beyond Quebec

ledger.note: 1763 (10 February): the occupation of the rest of Canada ends in cession.

region.text: Canada with all its dependencies: the Saint Lawrence valley, the Great Lakes and Ohio posts, New Brunswick and eastern Maine

ledger.note: 1763 (10 February): France cedes Canada. Treaty of Paris, Article IV: France 'cedes and guaranties to his said Britannick Majesty, in full right, Canada, with all its dependencies' (the Acadia page adds New Brunswick and Maine east of the Kennebec, 'Lost to Great Britain in 1763').

region.text: Cape Breton Island and the islands of the Gulf of St. Lawrence

ledger.note: 1763 (10 February): France cedes Cape Breton and the islands of the Gulf. Article IV: 'as well as the island of Cape Breton' and 'all the other islands and coasts in the gulph and river of St. Lawrence'; the page does not name Ile Saint-Jean, which the second phrase covers by my reading.

region.text: Louisiana east of the Mississippi: Mobile, the Gulf coast and the Illinois Country's east bank

ledger.note: 1763 (10 February): Louisiana east of the Mississippi goes to Britain. Article VII cedes 'every thing which he possesses, or ought to possess, on the left side of the river Mississippi', with 'the river and port of the Mobile', the line running 'along the middle of the River Mississippi, from its source to the river Iberville'. The Illinois Country page: the British took Fort de Chartres on 10 October 1765. Louisiana's Florida parishes north of the Iberville are on the east bank and are treated as part of this land here.

region.text: all of New France: Canada, Acadia, Ile Royale and Louisiana

ledger.note: 1763: New France ends. Treaty of Paris, 10 February 1763: 'By the Treaty of Paris, Louis XV cedes New France to Great Britain' (New France page); Canada and the east bank of Louisiana go to Britain, the west bank and New Orleans went to Spain in 1762, and France keeps Saint-Pierre and Miquelon and its Newfoundland fishing rights.

wars.name: Anglo-French War (1627-1629)
wars.outcome: English victory on the ground: David Kirke's fleet forced Quebec to surrender on 19 July 1629 after the treaty of Susa; the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye of 29 March 1632 returned Quebec, Acadia and Cape Breton Island.
wars.note: The Cape Breton page names 'the 1627-1629 Anglo-French War' and says the Kirkes 'planted a colony on Unama'ki at Baleine' which the French 'quickly defeated'; the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye page carries the Quebec surrender and the return.

wars.name: King William's War

zones.text: Acadia, with the Kennebec River as the southern border New France claimed

wars.outcome: No border change: 'At the end of the war in 1697, England returned the territory to France in the Treaty of Ryswick'; Acadia had been 'notionally integrated into the newly formed Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691'.
wars.note: The page dates the war only through '1688-97: New France defined the southern border as the Kennebec River'. Phips's 1690 capture of Port-Royal is mentioned without a date; the war's Hudson Bay front is in the next entry.

wars.name: Hudson Bay conflict (1686-1713)

zones.text: the Hudson's Bay Company posts on James Bay and Hudson Bay, York Factory

wars.outcome: French raids took the James Bay posts in 1686 and York Factory in 1694 (recovered by the company in 1695) and 1697; 'The French retained all of the outposts except Fort Albany until 1713', when Utrecht made France 'relinquish all claims to Great Britain on the Hudson Bay'.
wars.note: The page names 'the Battle of Hudson's Bay (5 September 1697)' and is silent on the Treaty of Ryswick.

wars.name: Queen Anne's War
wars.outcome: British victory: Acadia 'was conquered in 1710 during Queen Anne's War' and Utrecht (11 April 1713) ceded Nova Scotia, the Newfoundland claims and the Hudson Bay territories, while France kept Cape Breton Island.
wars.note: The first year of fighting is not on the pages opened; 1710 is the date the Acadia page gives for the conquest. The Treaty of Utrecht page carries the cessions.

wars.name: French and Indian War

zones.text: the Ohio Country and the forks of the Ohio
Fort Beauséjour, the Isthmus of Chignecto
Quebec and its district, the city that surrendered

wars.outcome: British victory: Fort Beauséjour (June 1755), Louisbourg (26 July 1758 per the Ile-Royale page), Quebec (September 1759) and Montreal (8 September 1760) fell; the Treaty of Paris of 10 February 1763 ceded Canada, Cape Breton and Louisiana east of the Mississippi, and Louisiana west of the river had gone to Spain.
wars.note: The page is silent on the dates of Louisbourg, Fort Frontenac, Fort Duquesne, Niagara and the surrender of Quebec; the Forbes Expedition is dated 'September-October 1758'. Pontiac's War (1763) is outside the state's life.

certainty.note: Settlements, forts and claims, not surveyed lines: the Pays d'en Haut and Ohio posts are points in Indigenous land, the Kennebec River claim was contested, and the Utrecht page names no boundary commission for Acadia or Hudson Bay. Louisiana was claimed 'from the Appalachian Mountains to the Rocky Mountains' while Cliopatria draws only the settled belt.
The Treaty of Paris fixed the Mississippi line 'along the middle of the River Mississippi, from its source to the river Iberville' and then Lakes Maurepas and Pontchartrain to the sea.

notes:
SCOPE. Cliopatria's 'New France' row (1609-1791) is not New France as the Wikipedia article defines it ('five colonies' in 1712: Canada, Acadia, Hudson Bay, Terre-Neuve, Louisiana). Counting H3 cells, about one quarter of every shape is French colonies elsewhere: Maranhao in Brazil (1612-1625), Saint Martin (1626-1631), Guadeloupe and Martinique (1636-), Fort-Dauphin in Madagascar (1645-1672), Grenada (1653-), Saint-Louis in Senegal (1659-), Saint-Domingue and Cayenne (1670-), Reunion (1670-1672), the Ivory Coast (1691-), the Seychelles (1757-1761) and Guyana (1783-1790). This dossier keeps only the Canadian and United States cells (verdict adjust, correction 'intersect with Canada and the United States'). Saint-Domingue and French Guiana already have dossiers (saint-domingue 1659-1791, french-colony-of-guiana 1643-1946, both written by am-06-x); every other overseas piece has none and will vanish from the map unless a gap-filler gives it one: French West Indies (Guadeloupe, Martinique, Saint Martin, Grenada, the Grenadines), French Senegal, Fort-Dauphin and Reunion, the Ivory Coast posts, France Equinoxiale (Maranhao), the Seychelles, and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (the only North American land France kept in 1763; Cliopatria draws it as the 1791 shape of this row and again in 1805-1814 as 'First French colonial empire').

START AND END. Cliopatria starts in 1609 and ends in 1791. The dossier starts in 1604 (Saint Croix Island) and ends on 10 February 1763 (Treaty of Paris, 'Ceded to Britain: 10 February 1763'); the 1763-1791 shapes are marked wrong because they are Spanish Louisiana (spanish-louisiana, from November 1762), Saint-Domingue, Guiana and the other overseas pieces. New France is empty (no land) in 1629-1631 (English held Quebec, Acadia and Cape Breton) and the keyframes use 'a region minus itself' for an empty shape.

PAGE DISAGREEMENTS. (1) Utrecht: the New France page dates it 1713 in places and 1715 in others; the Treaty of Utrecht page, the Acadia page and the Ile-Royale page say 1713. (2) Louisiana's capital moved to New Orleans in 1722 on the infobox and in the body and in 1723 in the timeline; the dossier does not use it. (3) Cape Breton in 1629: the treaty page says the English 'had seized' Cape Breton in 1629; the Cape Breton page has French settlements at Englishtown (1629) and St. Peter's (1630) and a Scottish colony at Baleine that the French 'quickly defeated'; the Acadia page dates English control of Acadia from 1621. The ledger follows the treaty page (loss 1629, gain 1632). (4) Cahokia: 1696 on the Illinois Country page, 1699 in Cliopatria's usual story; the page is followed. (5) Placentia: 'made Placentia (Plaisance) their capital' in 1655 and 'built Fort Plaisance in 1662' on the same page; 1662 is used. (6) The Illinois Country page gives Marquette's mission as 1675.
